chapter: South America and back in New York
title: Barcelona: the claque that must be paid
summary: In Barcelona the audience heckles until a fan explains the claque; the producer pays the claque man and the show goes down well.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So, anyhow, everything went very fine in Switzerland. So we moved on to Spain. Now, we be coming up to Spain, and we opened up in Barcelona, you see.
Is this now -- going back -- is this while the show is still with you?
The show is with us.
Right.
The show is with us. It's 1925. The show didn't close until after we came -- in 1926, after we came out of Russia.
I see. Is it -- is this the original
This is the original show. No, this is the original show.
The good one. Right.
So, now we start. Because they really started watering down in Vienna.
Uh hunh.

And that was after we come out of there. So, the funny part of it was, when we got to the -- we've been having a tremendous success everywhere. So we thought that Spain would be a pushover. So we thought. So we go into Barcelona, I don't remember the theater now -- I remember the theater in Madrid was the Infanta Beatriz. But in Barcelona, I don't remember the theater. Anyhow, we opened up. When the band --
Was it the Olympia Theater?
It could have been the Olympia. It could have been the Olympia.
The Olympia or the Casino San Sebastien?
Yeah, well, it wasn't in San Sebastien. That was the casino in San Sebastien. In Barcelona it was the Olympia. Now here's what happened.
When we played, we usually got a standing ovation everywhere. And we'd been spoiled by that. When we finished the opening of the overture. This time, when we finished the overture,

we got a lot of catcalls. "Meow, meow." Like that. So we still don't know what's happening. Now, when the show opens up, we begin to get more catcalls. So we weathered the storm. So when we come off the stage, a fellow that was a fan of us, came around behind the stage and says, "What's happening, what's the matter with you fellows?" "Did they take care of the claque?" It's the first time I heard the word 'claque', you know?
(laugh)

I said, "What claque?" He said, "You know, when you go to play in Spain and Italy, you're going to run on a claque, and if the director or you don't satisfy with a certain amount of money, you in trouble. The show is in trouble." And they could close the show, because they'd keep on -- everybody'd throw some dead cats up on the stage or something like that. So, anyhow, I went to Sirota, and I said, "Listen, have you done anything about the claque?" And he says, "Yes, some of them come to me and said they wanted some money for the show. But I told them I didn't need them, the show was good and people would enjoy it. So let it go." So I said, "You'd better go and find that man and give him some money. Because otherwise the band and the people in the show don't want to go on. Because they know what's happening, and we don't want to go out there and face them." So he sent someone, one of the Spanish fellows around there. He sent him out and he got this man and he satisfied him. We went out then and the show went
down lovely. You see, I mention that because we in America knew nothing about claques.
